blocks.text: Causal language modeling loss applies cross-entropy loss, covered in the previous topic, to the specific task of next token prediction, computed at every position across a sequence, and it is the loss function that actually powers the vast majority of the decoder model fine-tuning covered throughout this course.

This topic connects the general cross-entropy idea directly to the practical mechanics of training a decoder model, including how label masking, covered earlier in the Tokenization Pipeline topic, fits into the calculation.
1. What Causal Language Modeling Loss Measures

blocks.alt: What Causal Language Modeling Loss Measures
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959038-808073215.png

At every position in a sequence, a decoder model predicts a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for what token comes next, and causal language modeling loss applies cross-entropy at that position, comparing the model prediction against the actual token that really came next in the training data.
2. Next Token Prediction as the Underlying Task

blocks.alt: Next Token Prediction as the Underlying Task
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959284-469516385.png

Rather than computing loss just once for an entire sequence, causal language modeling computes a separate cross-entropy loss at every single position in that sequence, then typically averages those per position losses together to get one overall loss value for the sequence, or the batch, as a whole.
3. The Role of Label Masking
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959284-355040541.png

For supervised fine-tuning specifically, covered in the earlier SFT module, loss is typically only computed over the response or completion tokens, not the prompt tokens, exactly the label masking mechanism introduced in the Tokenization Pipeline topic, ensuring the model is only being trained to predict the parts it is actually meant to generate.

code.content:
# A simplified causal LM loss with label masking
predictions = model(input_ids)
losses = cross_entropy(predictions, labels, reduction="none")
masked_losses = losses * loss_mask  # zero out prompt positions
final_loss = masked_losses.sum() / loss_mask.sum()

blocks.text: 4. Why This Loss Powers Both Pretraining and Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Why This Loss Powers Both Pretraining and Fine-Tuning
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959285-218511591.png

Causal language modeling loss is exactly the same mechanism used during pretraining, covered in the Pretraining vs Fine-Tuning topic, and during fine-tuning, the difference between the two stages lies in the dataset and, for fine-tuning, the added label masking, not in the underlying loss calculation itself.
5. Perplexity, A Related Way to Read This Loss

blocks.alt: Perplexity, A Related Way to Read This Loss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959285-420862201.png

Perplexity, a commonly reported metric alongside raw loss, is simply the exponentiated version of the average cross-entropy loss, a number that can be interpreted roughly as how many equally likely choices the model was effectively uncertain between at each position, lower perplexity meaning more confident, accurate predictions.

blocks.text: 6. Loss Per Token vs Loss Per Sequence

blocks.alt: Loss Per Token vs Loss Per Sequence
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959285-178457432.png

Reporting loss as an average per token makes it comparable across sequences of different lengths, while summing loss across an entire sequence would naturally produce a larger number for longer sequences purely due to length, not necessarily because the model performed any worse, which is why per token averaging is the standard convention.
7. Common Causes of an Unexpectedly High Loss

blocks.alt: Common Causes of an Unexpectedly High Loss
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785471959285-811975663.png

A causal language modeling loss that stays surprisingly high throughout training often points back to a bug in an earlier stage, incorrect label masking accidentally including prompt tokens in the loss, or a mismatched chat template, covered in the Dataset Preparation module, feeding the model input it was never trained to expect.

blocks.title: This is the practical payoff of understanding the loss mechanism in depth
blocks.content: Knowing exactly how causal language modeling loss is computed, including label masking, makes it far easier to diagnose why a training run loss looks wrong, rather than treating the loss value as an unexplained black box number.

blocks.text: 8. Causal Loss and the Attention Mask

The causal masking covered in the earlier Decoder Models topic, which prevents a position from seeing future tokens, and the label masking used for loss computation are related but distinct concepts, one controls what the model can see during the forward pass, the other controls which positions actually contribute to the training loss.
9. Sequence Packing and Causal Loss

When using sequence packing, covered in the Dataset Preparation module, causal language modeling loss needs to be computed correctly per packed example within the shared sequence, respecting the same cross-example isolation that the attention mask maintains, so loss from one packed example never bleeds into another.
Worked Example

A team notices their fine-tuned model loss plateaus at a surprisingly high value early in training and never improves much further. Investigating their label masking implementation, they discover it was accidentally including prompt tokens in the loss calculation, diluting the training signal with content the model was never meant to learn to generate.

After correcting the masking to only compute loss over the intended response tokens, retraining produces a loss curve that decreases steadily to a much lower final value, confirming the earlier plateau was specifically a label masking bug rather than a genuine limit on how well the model could learn the task.
Common Mistakes

items: Including prompt tokens in the loss calculation instead of masking them out for supervised fine-tuning
Comparing raw summed loss across sequences of different lengths instead of using per token averaged loss
Confusing causal attention masking, which controls visibility, with label masking, which controls loss computation
Not checking label masking or chat template correctness as an early diagnostic step when loss looks unexpectedly high

blocks.text: Practice

For a short training example with a prompt and a response, sketch which tokens should have loss computed and which should be masked out, confirming you understand exactly where the label mask boundary belongs in a supervised fine-tuning example.
Key Takeaway

Causal language modeling loss applies cross-entropy at every position in a sequence to the task of next token prediction, typically averaged per token and, for supervised fine-tuning, masked so only the intended response tokens actually contribute, making it the specific loss mechanism underlying both pretraining and the vast majority of fine-tuning covered throughout this course.
